newsitem.title: USA: Will the Simpson "gravy train" grind to a halt?
newsitem.headline: Will the Simpson "gravy train" grind to a halt?

text.p: During closing arguments in the O.J. Simpson civil trial, defence attorney Robert Baker attacked the media for riding "the gravy train."
But despite Tuesday's verdict finding Simpson liable for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend, there was no sign the gravy train was screeching to a halt.
The O.J. express has been chugging along on a sensational ride for 2-1/2 years with all kinds of passengers hanging on, including, though Baker didn't mention it, members of his own profession.
As for the public's appetite for a case that has it all -- glamour, sex, celebrity, sports -- the jury is still out.

"It's difficult to know what the aftermath of this latest verdict will be. Will it (the case) fade away or stay in the mind?" said John Baker, a senior editor at Publisher's Weekly, commenting on the explosion of books written about the case.
Simpson's 1995 televised criminal trial, at which he was acquitted of the two murders, made instant stars of lawyers, jurors, journalists, police and anyone remotely involved.
Some made it big, but for others, the spotlight may be as brief as an Andy Warhol 15 minutes of fame.

One-time Simpson pal, Brian "Kato" Kaelin, who became known during the criminal trial as "the world's most famous house-guest," briefly had a radio show. But he is still a struggling actor and was seen recently on a TV dating game.

Time will tell if Daniel Petrocelli, lead plaintiffs' attorney in the civil trial, will become a media darling like his predecessors in the criminal trial, or if Simpson's lawyer, the perpetually-tanned Baker, will hit the lecture circuit.
Despite the lack of cameras at the civil case, there has been no shortage of public attention this time round, with everyone being courted by TV, newspapers and book publishers.
Faye Resnick, a friend of Nicole Brown Simpson, can currently be seen draped naked across the pages of Playboy. She also wrote a book about the relationship between Simpson and his ex-wife.
Another fringe player was Tracy Hampton, who was a criminal trial juror before being excused for ill-health. She took it all off for Playboy, but her fledgling acting career has not taken off.

Model Paula Barbieri, the girfriend who broke up with Simpson the morning before Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were butchered to death, has also appeared in men's magazines. Now she has signed to write a book for a reported $3.5 million.
"It's a tremendous gamble (by publisher Little Brown) because she was not involved (in the murders). I can't think what she can say," said Baker, of Publisher's Weekly.
He noted there had been about 40 books about the Simpson case, and the publishing industry was still prepared to offer large advances despite some notable failures.
Johnny Cochran, the eloquent defence lawyer who won Simpson's acquittal on murder charges, has landed himself a job co-hosting a legal show on Court TV.
He also made some $4 million for a book about the case, although neither it, nor a book by Simpson attorney Robert Shapiro, sold as well as expected, Baker said.

Criminal prosecutor Christopher Darden's tome was a hot-seller and a volume by Tom Lange and Philip Vannatter, two of the homicide detectives assigned to the case, just came out in time for the civil trial verdict.

At least their books have seen the light of day. Lead criminal trial prosecutor Marcia Clark, who joined a top Hollywood agency after losing the so-called "Trial of the Century", signed a book deal reportedly worth $4.2 million.
"The world is still waiting for it, some 16 months later. It's been a long time in preparation, but I think it will be something that goes beyond O.J. into a woman's life today," Baker said.
Clark is reportedly having trouble convincing TV stations to buy the syndicated show about women in law enforcement that she has been signed up to anchor.

Some TV shows however, owe their existence to the first Simpson trial. Lawyer Greta van Susteren appeared on CNN as a legal commentator for the criminal trial and now co-hosts the cable network's biggest-rated daytime show, "Burden of Proof" which examines legal issues in the news.
And Geraldo Rivera's CNBC show, built around the Simpson case, set ratings records for the cable station for Tuesday night's verdict.
